newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil economy doing well, says government.
newsitem.headline: Brazil economy doing well, says government.

text.p: Half way through its term, the Brazilian government on Saturday painted a rosy picture of its economic achievements and sketched out its policy priorities for the next two years.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and his ministers, in a special cabinet meeting, listed record foreign investment, privatization proceeds and healthy growth as signs Brazil was on a path out of past economic turmoil, officials said.
"The president said the trend is certainly positive," presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral reported in a briefing at Cardoso's official country estate just outside Brasilia.
"The problems we face are normal but what's important is that the government is succeeding in overcoming those difficulties and is achieving its objectives."

Amaral, quoting Finance Minister Pedro Malan, said Brazil was on course for 3.0 percent gross domestic product (GDP) growth this year and 4.5 to 5.0 percent growth in 1997, exceeding Malan's own estimates a month ago of 3.5 to 4.0 percent GDP growth in 1997.

Amaral said Malan had projected a current account deficit for this year of 2.9 percent of GDP and, despite market unease at Brazil's burgeoning trade deficit, this was well below the current account gaps of similar countries.

In the cabinet meeting, Planning Minister Antonio Kandir reported that Brazil expected to receive a record $8 billion in net foreign direct investment this year and up to $12 billion in 1997. In 1995, Brazil received just under $4 billion in investment.

The president's chief of staff, Clovis Carvalho, summing up for various ministries, said privatization proceeds in 1996 would be a record $4.5 billion, up from the previous record in 1993 when state sell-offs netted Brazil $2.7 billion.
But the cabinet also acknowledged Brazil still had much to do to distance itself from the hyperinflation and stop-go economic activity of the recent past.
Finance Minister Malan identified Brazil's inability to balance its public books as the chief concern.
"No doubt it is in the fiscal area where the greatest challenge lies," Amaral said.

Latin America's largest country last year posted an operational public sector deficit of almost 5.0 percent of GDP but it failed in efforts to halve that in 1996. Officials predict the deficit will hit at least 3.5 percent of GDP this year.

Malan said that any improvement in the fiscal accounts depended on approval of key reforms of the state pension system and civil service by Congress, which has proven uneager to slash the public sector pay perks it itself enjoys.
According to Amaral, Cardoso also listed progress on human rights, land reform and wealth distribution as achievements of his government, which took power in January 1995.

Not only had the "Plano Real" economic stablization plan cut inflation to about 13 percent this year and thereby boosted the buying power of the poor, but Brasilia had also directed half its resources to health and other social services.
A recent United Nations report said Brazil had one of the most unequal distributions of wealth in the world and critics say Cardoso has not done enough for the dispossessed.
But Amaral said progress had been made, adding: "There is, of course, still a long way to go."
